body.text: Miguel Angel Félix Gallardo, 80, founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels and whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers, died on November 15.

The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier. “After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility” after “he suffered multiple organ failure,” according to a statement from the Security Ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.

Gallardo’s health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes, and deafness. In 2022, then-President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was “in very poor health”. A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.

Gallardo was a native of Sinaloa state, where he was born on January 8, 1946, according to public records. His involvement in crime went virtually hand in hand with his career in the state and federal police. Gallardo even served as a bodyguard to a Sinaloa Governor, a role that experts say may have helped him secure the complicity and protection of powerful politicians.

He partnered with another veteran kingpin, Rafael Caro Quintero. Together with other crime bosses, they united gangs trafficking drugs to the United States and formed the Guadalajara cartel. The cartel was formed around a “hegemonic model” and laid “the roots for nearly all of today’s drug trafficking activities,” according to InSight Crime, a website specialising in the drug trade. Gallardo “partnered with Colombian traffickers like Pablo Escobar and became Escobar’s most important Mexico associate,” the publication said.
The Guadalajara gang controlled the country’s underworld, earning Gallardo the nicknames “El jefe de jefes” and “El Padrino”—which translate to “the boss of bosses” and “the Godfather".

Gallardo was convicted for the February 1985 murder of Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured. The agent’s death remains an open wound for the US. Intense pressure from Washington led to the arrest in 1985 of Caro Quintero, who is now imprisoned in the US on charges of drug trafficking and the agent’s murder.

Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to control the criminal business from prison, according to experts. He was serving his sentence at Puente Grande prison in Jalisco state. The Guadalajara cartel imploded in the 1990s, and its local leaders formed regional cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, built up by Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman and Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, both sentenced to life in prison in the US.

Gallardo remained in the popular imagination through narcocorridos, or drug ballads, such as “El jefe de jefes,” which is banned in public spaces, and the 2018 Netflix drama Narcos: Mexico about drug trafficking, with Mexican actor Diego Luna portraying the kingpin. He suffered poor health in his final years, and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.
“Thirty-two years have passed... That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime,” he said.
